entry:
[[Arithmetic]] operation on two numbers, the base *b* and the exponent *n*, written bⁿ. When *n* is a positive [[Integer|integer]], bⁿ is the product of [[Multiplication|multiplying]] *b* by itself *n* times, so that 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. The exponent is also called the power or, in British English, the index; b² and b³ are read "b squared" and "b cubed" because they give the area of a square and the volume of a cube.

The operation can be defined by induction as b¹ = b and bⁿ⁺¹ = bⁿ · b, and it obeys bᵐ⁺ⁿ = bᵐ · bⁿ and (bᵐ)ⁿ = bᵐⁿ. A number raised to the 0 power is generally defined as 1, which keeps the first rule valid when m = 0, although zero to the power of zero may be an exception depending on context. For nonzero b, negative exponents are defined by b⁻ⁿ = 1/bⁿ. Raising 0 to a negative exponent is typically undefined, though in some circumstances it may be interpreted as [[Infinity|infinity]].

Unlike addition and multiplication, exponentiation is neither commutative nor associative: 2³ = 8 but 3² = 9, and (2³)² = 64 whereas 2^(3²) = 2⁹ = 512.

The definition extends to any positive [[Real number|real]] base and real exponent, and a more involved definition supports [[Complex number|complex numbers]] as base and exponent. René Descartes introduced modern superscript notation in 1637, initially for positive integers greater than two. Exponentiation models [[Exponential function|exponential]] growth and decay, and modular exponentiation is used in cryptography.

Termination of a [[Species|species]] through the death of its last member. A taxon may become functionally extinct earlier if it loses the capacity to reproduce and recover. Because a species' range may be very large, the moment is usually identified retrospectively; this leads to Lazarus taxa, species presumed extinct that abruptly "reappear," typically in the [[Fossil|fossil]] record. Local extinction, in which a species vanishes from a study area but survives elsewhere, may be reversed by reintroduction, as with wolves.

Species become extinct when they can no longer survive changing conditions or superior [[Competition (biology)|competition]]. A typical species becomes extinct within 10 million years of its first appearance, although so-called living fossils survive with little change for hundreds of millions of years, a claim that has been disputed. Over five billion species are estimated to have died out, against about 8.7 million eukaryote species alive today. Isolated extinctions are common and natural, while mass extinctions are rare. The loss of a keystone species can cause further extinctions, called "chains of extinction." Species surviving only in [[Zoo|zoos]] or other artificial environments are listed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature as "extinct in the wild."

Contemporary extinctions are attributed largely to human activity, chiefly destruction of natural [[Habitat|habitats]]. A 2019 assessment by IPBES reported that the biomass of wild mammals had fallen by 82%, natural ecosystems had lost about half their area, and a million species were at risk. At least 571 plant species have been lost since 1750. Whether this amounts to a sixth mass extinction is debated; critics cite undocumented extinctions and incomplete taxonomic inventories as sources of uncertainty.

Sensory organ that detects light and converts it into electrochemical impulses in [[Neuron|neurons]], forming part of an organism's visual system. In higher organisms it is a complex optical system that regulates the intensity of light, focuses it through adjustable lenses to form an image, and sends electrical signals along the optic nerve to the visual cortex and other brain areas.

Eyes with resolving power have come in ten fundamentally different forms, classified as compound or non-compound. Non-compound, or simple, eyes have a single lens that focuses light onto the retina and are common in mammals, including humans. In most vertebrates and some molluscs, cone cells (for color) and rod cells (for low-light contrasts) in the retina convert light into neural signals. The eyes of most [[Cephalopod|cephalopods]], fish, amphibians, and snakes focus by telescoping a fixed-shape lens, as in a [[Camera|camera]]. The simplest eyes, such as the ocelli of some snails, distinguish only light from dark.

[[Compound eye|Compound eyes]], common in insects and crustaceans, consist of many small visual units, each with its own lens and photosensitive cells. Some have up to 28,000 sensors arranged hexagonally, giving a full 360° field of vision; they are very sensitive to motion, but their physics limits resolution to no better than 1°. The extinct [[Trilobite|trilobites]] had clear calcite lenses, from one to thousands per eye. The [[Mantis shrimp|mantis shrimp]] has the most complex color vision system known.

The first proto-eyes evolved about 600 million years ago, about the time of the [[Cambrian explosion]].

Group of people related by [[Consanguinity|consanguinity]] (recognized birth) or [[Affinity (law)|affinity]] (marriage or other relationship). The word derives from Latin *familia*. The family forms the basis for [[Social order|social order]]. Ideally it offers predictability, structure, and safety as members mature and learn to participate in the community, and historically most human societies have treated it as the primary setting for attachment, nurturance, and socialization.

Anthropologists classify most family organizations as matrifocal (a mother and her children), patrifocal (a father and his children), conjugal (a married couple with children, also called the [[Nuclear family|nuclear family]]), avuncular (a man, his sister, and her children), or extended (parents, spouse, and children, plus grandparents, aunts, uncles, or cousins). Historically the most common type was the multigenerational family, in which grandparents, parents, and children live as one unit. In the U.S. this arrangement declined after World War II to a low in 1980, when about one in eight people lived in such a family, and had risen to one in five by 2016; in Canada the figure was about 6% in 2016. A single-parent family consists of one parent and children, the parent being widowed, divorced, or never married.

One primary function of the family is to provide a framework for the biological and social production and reproduction of persons, through shared food, care and nurture, legal rights and obligations, and moral and sentimental ties. From a child's perspective it is a "family of orientation," which shapes enculturation; from a parent's perspective it is a "family of procreation." In societies with a sexual division of labor, marriage is also necessary for forming an economically productive household. Early Western anthropologists tied family to "blood" relations, but later research found that many societies instead understand family through living together and sharing food and care. Steven Ruggles's analysis of census data suggests that 19th-century Northwest Europe and North America did not have exceptionally simple or nuclear family structures.

Who counts as family is disputed. C. C. Harris notes that the Western conception is ambiguous and confused with the household, and a survey asking Americans about 11 household structures found a wide variety of answers. As of 2015 the total fertility rate ranged from 6.76 children per woman in Niger to 0.81 in Singapore, with rates below replacement in all Eastern and Southern European countries and particularly high in Sub-Saharan Africa. Some researchers link stable two-parent biological families to better child outcomes; redefinitions of the family beyond biological ties remain contested.

Widespread scarcity of food, usually accompanied or followed by regional [[Malnutrition|malnutrition]], starvation, epidemic, and increased mortality. Causes include war, natural disasters, crop failure, poverty, and government policies. Every inhabited continent has experienced famine; the Americas have been among the least affected. In the 19th and 20th centuries, [[China]], India, Europe, and the Middle East suffered the greatest number of famine deaths. Deaths declined sharply from the 1970s and have fallen further since 2000, though Haiti, Afghanistan, Sudan, Yemen, Gaza, and Syria are among places that have experienced famine.

Under the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, famine (Phase 5) exists when three conditions coincide: at least 20% of households in an area face extreme food shortages with limited ability to cope; acute malnutrition in children exceeds 30%; and the death rate exceeds two people per 10,000 per day. A declaration carries no binding obligations on the [[United Nations]] or member states but focuses global attention.

Famine recurred cyclically in societies practicing [[Subsistence agriculture|subsistence agriculture]]. As the feudal system broke down in the 16th and 17th centuries, commercialized farming and taxes paid in money pushed production toward the market. By the 1590s the province of Holland, in the [[Netherlands]], could withstand a famine that struck Western Europe, and in [[England]] the last peacetime famine was in 1623–24.

Analysts differ on emphasis. Economist Amartya Sen's entitlement approach holds that famines arise from breakdowns in people's rights to obtain food, not merely from shortfalls in supply, and he observed that no substantial famine has afflicted a functioning [[Democracy|democracy]] with a free press. One account attributes the deadliest famines of the 20th century to state-driven collectivization in the [[Soviet Union]] and China, with estimates of 5–10 million and 30–45 million deaths respectively.

Far-right, authoritarian, and ultranationalist political ideology and movement that rose to prominence in early 20th-century Europe. Scholars generally describe it as characterized by a dictatorial leader, centralized autocracy, [[Militarism|militarism]], forcible suppression of opposition, belief in a natural social hierarchy, subordination of the individual to the perceived interest of the nation or race, and strong regimentation of society and the economy. It opposed [[Communism|communism]], democracy, liberalism, pluralism, and socialism. What constitutes a precise definition has been a long-running scholarly debate; the historian Ian Kershaw wrote that defining it is "like trying to nail jelly to the wall."

The name comes from Italian *fascio*, "bundle," and the ancient Roman fasces, a bundle of rods tied around an axe that symbolized strength through unity. [[Benito Mussolini]] founded the Italian Fasces of Combat in [[Milan]] in 1919; it became the National Fascist Party two years later. The first fascist movements emerged in Italy during [[World War I]] before spreading elsewhere, most notably to Germany. Mussolini took power after the March on Rome in October 1922 and by 1925 had consolidated dictatorial authority. Italian doctrine promoted corporatism, organizing society into state-supervised syndicates.

Fascism often centered on opposition to "Others," such as ethnic groups, immigrants, and political opponents; in [[Nazism]] this involved racial purity and a belief in a master race. Fascist regimes committed massacres and genocides, and during [[World War II]] the ambitions of the [[Axis powers]] resulted in the murder of millions. Defenders of Italian fascism point to public works and reduced unemployment, while critics stress the murder of the socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti in 1924, press censorship, and the 1938 racial laws. Since 1945 fascism has been largely disgraced; few parties describe themselves as fascist, and the term is often used pejoratively.

Creation, mixing, and wearing of clothing, footwear, accessories, cosmetics, and jewelry in distinctive styles that signify social status, self-expression, and group belonging. The term, from Latin *facere*, "to make," can describe an industry, designs, aesthetics, and trends.

Fashion differs from related ideas. A trend is a short-lived aesthetic expression, often lasting less than a season; fashion is an industry-supported expression tied to the fashion season and its collections; style lasts over many seasons and connects to cultural movements, such as [[Baroque]] and [[Rococo]]. The sociologist [[Pierre Bourdieu]] described fashion as "the latest difference." Fashion also differs from [[Clothing|clothing]], the material garment without social meaning, and from [[Costume|costume]], which has come to mean fancy dress. What is fashionable may be defined by an elite of fashion houses and haute couturiers, yet their looks are often drawn from [[Subculture|subcultures]] outside that elite. In France, haute couture is technically limited to members of the Chambre Syndicale de la Haute Couture in Paris.

The four leading fashion capitals are recognized as New York City, London, Milan, and Paris, in the chronological order of their fashion weeks, where designers exhibit new collections. One estimate valued the global fashion market at $1.84 trillion in 2025, about 1.65% of world GDP.

[[Mass production]] at lower prices and global reach has made environmental impact and sustainability pressing concerns for politicians, brands, and consumers. Critics point to water use in dyeing, microfiber pollution from synthetic garments, a share of global carbon emissions estimated at 10%, and labor conditions in outsourcing hubs.

[[Emotion|Emotional]] state aroused by threatening situations, usually regarded as negative and unpleasant. Fear can result directly from sensory stimulation, such as sounds resembling screaming, from anticipating that undesirable events may occur, or from imagining threats that may not be real.

In humans, fear is correlated with more rapid breathing and heart rate, dilation of the pupils, spikes in [[Cortisol|cortisol]] levels, and elevated electrodermal activity, changes that overlap considerably with other negative, arousing emotions. Behavioral reactions include the startle, fight-or-flight, and freeze responses. The amygdala serves as a central hub for threat detection, interfacing with the hypothalamus and [[Brainstem|brainstem]] to trigger release of [[Adrenaline|adrenaline]]. Fear is distinguished from [[Anxiety|anxiety]], a diffuse, future-oriented apprehension, by its focus on specific, proximate stimuli. Its subjective experience is shaped by individual differences, situational factors, and culture, and it may be pleasurable and deliberately sought in thrilling activities and horror films. Maladaptive levels are associated with specific [[Phobia|phobias]] and with depression, anxiety, and suicidality.

Although many fears are learned, the capacity to fear is part of human nature, and certain fears, such as of animals and heights, are far more common and easier to induce than others, such as of flowers or clouds. This phenomenon, called preparedness, is theorized to be a genetic effect of [[Natural selection|natural selection]]. From an [[Evolutionary psychology|evolutionary psychology]] perspective, fear of heights may be common to all mammals and fear of snakes to all simians.

Fear conditioning was first studied in John B. Watson's Little Albert experiment in 1920, in which an 11-month-old boy was conditioned to fear a white rat; the fear generalized to other white, furry objects, including a rabbit, a dog, and a Santa Claus mask.

Range of socio-political movements and ideologies that aim to establish the political, economic, personal, and social equality of the sexes. Feminism holds that modern societies are patriarchal, prioritizing the male point of view, and that women are treated unjustly in them. Originating in late 18th-century Europe, feminist movements have campaigned for the right to vote, run for office, work, earn equal pay, own property, receive education, and enter into contracts, as well as for access to contraception and legal [[Abortion|abortion]] and protection from sexual assault, sexual harassment, and domestic violence.

[[Mary Wollstonecraft]] is seen by many as a founder of feminism because of her 1792 book [[A Vindication of the Rights of Woman|*A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*]], which argued that women as much as men needed equal rights. The word *féminisme* first appeared in France in 1871, and the *Oxford English Dictionary* dates the English use in this sense to 1895; early uses were negative.

Many scholars consider feminist campaigns a main force behind historical changes in women's rights, particularly in the West, where they are widely credited with achieving [[Women's suffrage|women's suffrage]], reproductive rights, and the right to own property. The movement is commonly described in "waves": the first focused on suffrage and property rights, the second on employment discrimination and reproductive autonomy from the mid-20th century, the third on identity and representation from the 1990s, and the fourth on digital activism since the 2010s. Liberal, socialist, and radical feminism are sometimes called the "Big Three" schools. Some newer forms have been criticized for reflecting only white, middle-class, or heterosexual perspectives, prompting black and intersectional feminism. Critics argue that feminism underappreciates biological sex differences, a claim supporters dispute.

Natural or synthetic material applied to soil or plant tissues to supply plant nutrients. Modern practice centers on three macronutrients: [[Nitrogen|nitrogen]] (N), [[Phosphorus|phosphorus]] (P), and [[Potassium|potassium]] (K). Historically, fertilization relied on compost, animal and human manure, harvested minerals, crop rotation, and byproducts such as fish waste and bloodmeal.

In the 19th century, following discoveries by [[Justus von Liebig]], an industry developed around synthetic fertilizers. John Bennet Lawes began experimenting with manures in 1837 and in 1842 patented a manure made by treating phosphates with sulfuric acid, founding the artificial manure industry. The Birkeland–Eyde process, which fixed atmospheric nitrogen into nitric acid, was an early competitor, with factories built in Norway. In the 1910s and 1920s the [[Haber process]], which makes ammonia from natural gas and nitrogen in air, came to dominate. Wartime plants were redirected to agriculture after World War II, and nitrogen fertilizer use rose by 800% between 1961 and 2019, a crucial component of the [[Green Revolution]]. Phosphate use rose from 9 million tonnes per year in 1960 to 40 million in 2000. In 2021, agricultural use of inorganic fertilizers was 195 million tonnes of nutrients, of which 56% was nitrogen; Asia accounted for 53%.

It is estimated that a third of annual global food production uses ammonia from the Haber–Bosch process and that synthetic nitrogen feeds almost half the world's population. Excessive application can cause [[Water pollution|water pollution]] and eutrophication through nutrient runoff, and production emits carbon and other byproducts. Some mined fertilizers accumulate heavy metals in soil. Reduced tillage and planting buffer strips can limit these effects.
